John Hay. Secretary of State under President Theodore Roosevelt from 1901 to 1905, a pivotal figure in establishing American dominance in the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific. His diplomacy brought the United States into the First Hague Peace Conference, negotiated the construction of the Panama Canal, and formulated the Open Door Policy toward China—foundational principles of American imperialism at the turn of the twentieth century.

Hay formulated the Open Door Policy between 1899 and 1900, asserting American commercial interests in China against European partition and Japanese expansion. He negotiated the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty in 1901 with Britain, which cleared the way for American construction of the Panama Canal. He then secured the Panama Canal Zone in 1903 through support for Panama's separation from Colombia, enabling United States control of this strategic waterway.

When the Boxer Rebellion erupted in 1900, Hay supported American intervention to protect American missionaries and commercial interests in China. Later, he mediated an end to the Russo-Japanese War in 1904 and 1905, an achievement that won him the Nobel Peace Prize and established American diplomatic weight in Asian affairs. Hay believed the United States should expand commerce and influence globally while remaining largely aloof from European entanglements.

Theodore Roosevelt was the president under whom Hay orchestrated American imperial expansion. The Panama Canal became his greatest achievement, reshaping world commerce and American power. His Open Door Policy was the diplomatic principle he crafted to preserve American access to Chinese markets. And the Boxer Rebellion tested American commitment to China during his tenure.
